newsitem.title: UK: Brazil frost, grower reserve hold key in coffee - GNI.
newsitem.headline: Brazil frost, grower reserve hold key in coffee - GNI.

text.p: The longer-term outlook for the coffee market, which has seen sharp price rise over the past months, hinged on Brazilian and Colombian stock disposals and the impending frost season in Brazil, UK broker GNI Ltd said.
It said the recent price rise by more than 50 percent on an exceptionally tight market has shocked many roasters, and several would be questioning the wisdom of their low stock policy.

With supplies from Brazil expected around 24 million bags in 1997/98, down from 27 million this season, coffee could be heading into a supply deficit again next year, it said in its latest Commodity Perspective report.
Production from Colombia, the world's top grower after Brazil, is uncertain and there is always the weather factor.
"Indeed should a frost occur in Brazil over the next 18 months, the impact on world prices could be shocking," it said.
Recent price action has shown that roaster stocks are at or below working minimums while producers swept the storerooms clean after the last Brazilian frosts in 1994.
Therefore the only reserves left for the free world at the moment are held by the Colombian Coffee Federation (six million bags) and the Brazilian government (13.2 million).

By September, these stocks should have been reduced to four and 11.1 million bags respectively and by the end of June 1998, further reductions may have been seen to three million and four to eight million respectively.
"That could leave the global coffee stockpile reserve as low as seven million bags -- not much of a buffer against a crop failure in one of the major producing countries," GNI said.
The UK house then outlined two possible scenarios for the market in the coming months.
It said the best outcome would be that the Brazilian and Colombian governments supply sufficient coffee to the market to keep prices in a $1.30-$1.50 a lb.
This would provide producers with a healthy renumeration while consumption growth would be maintained.
The worst case scenario would involve a frost of 1994's magnitude in Brazil this year, with production pared back to 15 million bags in 1998/99.
Complete liquidation of the Brazilian and Colombian stockpiles would leave the market in a deficit situation in 1998/99 of up to nine million bags.
"Coffee prices could then rise to more than $5 a lb (perhaps as high as $7)," it said.
Coffee is hovering at nearly $2.00 basis New York's March futures, up from $1.17 at the start of the year.
